newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rexrodt seeks wider acceptance of gene technology.
newsitem.headline: Rexrodt seeks wider acceptance of gene technology.

text.p: Genetic technology needs to be more widely accepted if German firms are to take full advantage of the potential benefits the industry offers, German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Monday.

"However, the level of acceptance of genetic technology among the population is a big problem," Rexrodt said in a speech delivered at a visit to the BASF genetic joint venture, BASF-LYNX Bioscience AG.
There was a particular problem in gaining acceptance for so-called green genetic technology among German agriculturists.

Genetic technology has been the subject of much controversy in recent months. A group of scientists in Britain recently genetically engineered, or "cloned", a sheep called Dolly, which led to much debate on the ethics of genetic technology.
But Rexrodt said that explanation of green genetic technology was necessary and that global ethical limits needed to be formulated and observed.

"Germany cannot afford to lose its connection to new technology. If we don't keep up with research and development in new technologies, then we will not be able to maintain our standards of living in the long-term," Rexrodt said.

Germany needed a sea change in how it viewed genetic technology. There are 150, mostly small and medium-sized, biotechnology companies with around 28,000 employees in Germany at the moment, with only six genetic technology production sites, Rexrodt said.
This compares with the U.S., where there are 1,300 such companies employing 118,000 people with 300 genetic technology production facilities.

Some forecasters say that increased focus on genetic technology in the pharmaceutical sector alone could double sales to 4.1 billion marks ($2.2 billion) with 100,000 employees in the sector, Rexrodt said.
The decision by BASF AG to form the joint venture in October 1996 with LYNX showed that BASF wanted to widen its engagement in biotechnology, BASF-Lynx management board chairman Alfred Bach said.
The joint venture employs 11 people at the moment, which the group expects to expand to 20 by the end of the year and 60 people in three years.
